## Methods

Constructs design
For subcellular localization: the coding sequence of nPME (Medtr2g105560), SyPG1 (Medtr2g032710) and SyPG2 (Medtr6g028080) were synthesized and then cloned into the GoldenGate EC50507 vector27, and Lotus ubiquitin (Ubi) promoter was used to drive the expression of those genes. For promoter activation: promoter sequences (2000 bp) of SyPG1 and SyPG2 were amplified by PCR from M. truncatula A17 genomic DNA and then ligated into the pCAMBIA1391 vector by Gibson assembly. For RNAi: the sequence was amplified and cloned into pZHY930 vector by Gibson assembly. For CRISPR gene editing, the amplified sequences were cloned into pGES402 vector via BsaI enzyme sites28. All primers used are listed in Supplementary Table 1.

Hairy root transformation
The constructs were transformed into the Agrobacterium rhizogenes (strR, CamR) ArQual strain and used for hairy root transformation as described previously29. In short, M. truncatula A17 seeds were surface-sterilized by sulfuric acid (10 min) and bleach solution (1.2% sodium hypochlorite, 0.1% sodium dodecyl sulfate; 60 s), with 5 times sterile water rinses between the two steps. Seeds were rinsed five additional times with sterile water before being plated on 1% agar plates and stratified at 4°C for 3 days. Subsequently, they were germinated overnight at 24°C in darkness and used for hairy root transformation. After transformation, the plants were kept in darkness at 24°C for 3 days and then in light at 24°C for 4 days (upper part of the plate only). Seedlings were then transferred to new Fahräeus medium plates (containing 0.5 mM NH4NO3) for an additional 10–14 days, and then positively transformed plants were identified with a portable fluorescent lamp (LUYOR-3415, American Router). The positive composite plants were then transferred to open pots (3:1 mix of vermiculite and perlite, 1 plant/pot) and grown in a greenhouse (12 h light/12 h dark, 25°C, light intensity 200 μmol/m2/s). Five days later, S. meliloti 2011 (OD600 = 0.03; 10 mL/plant) was used to inoculate the plants. Plants were harvested at 3 weeks post-inoculation for further analysis.

Technovit 8100 sectioning and Immunofluorescence
Nodules (3 wpi) were harvested and then immediately fixed in a PBS solution containing 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA) under vacuum for 15 min (twice) and stored at 4°C in the fixative solution overnight. They were then dehydrated in acetone/H2O graded series (50%, 70%, 80%, 90%, 100%, 1 h each at 4°C). Final dehydration in absolute acetone was repeated once, followed by incubation in acetone/Technovit infiltration solution (1:3, 2:2, 3:1, 60 min each at 4°C), and then the final infiltration in pure Technovit infiltration solution was carried out overnight at 4°C. Embedding of the samples was performed as directed by the manufacturer. Nodule sections (10 µm) for immunofluorescence labeling were obtained using a RM2155 microtome (Leica). The nodule sections were blocked with 3% BSA for 30 min at room temperature. Then the primary antibody (LM19 (2w00019S) and LM20 (2w00020s), from Abmart) was applied to the sections (1 to 50 diluted in PBS solution supplied with 3% BSA) and incubated for 1–2 h at room temperature. The sample was then washed at least 3 times (5 min each time) with PBS solution. The secondary antibody (conjugated with Alex Fluor 488 (A-11006), from Invitrogen) was then added diluted in PBS solution containing 3% BSA and then the sample was incubated for another 30 min to 1 h. The sample was then washed at least 3 times before images were taken. Note that after applying the secondary antibody all steps were performed in darkness. The samples were then imaged using a Leica SP8 confocal microscope.
For immuno-gold staining: the samples were embedded with LR White according to the protocol descript in Su et al.11. Goat-anti Rat IgG 10 nm gold conjugated polyclonal antibody (Sigma, G7035) was used as secondary antibody.

Technovit 7100 sections and GUS staining
The sample preparation followed same process described above for Technovit 8100, except that ethanol was used instead of acetone. The GUS staining was performed according to a previous study30. Briefly, tissue samples were collected in 5 mL tubes immersed in GUS staining solution, following vacuum twice for 10 min each time. The samples were incubated at 37°C for 4–8 h (in dark). After staining, the samples were cleared with 75% ethanol and stored in 75% ethanol for subsequent analysis. The stained nodules were embedded in Technovit 7100 for sectioning and visualization. All nodule sections were stained with 0.05% w/v Toluidine Blue or 0.1% w/v Ruthenium red prior to imaging. Images were taken with a ZEISS Axiolab 5 microscope.

In situ hybridization
Using specific primers (see Supplementary Table 1), the 254 bp sequence fragment of SyPG1 (corresponding to part of the coding sequence and the 3′ untranslated region) and the 251 bp coding sequence fragment of SyPG2 were amplified from cDNA using KOD polymerase (KFX-101, Stratagene, San Diego, CA). Subsequently, the amplified fragments were cloned into the pEASY®-Blunt3 vector (CB301-01, TransGen Biotech, San Diego, CA). Digoxigenin-labelled sense or antisense probes were synthesized using T7 or SP6 RNA polymerase. Medicago nodule samples were collected 7–10 days and 21 days post-inoculation. Following fixation in 4% PFA, the samples underwent paraffin embedding and sectioning at 8–10 µm thickness. After deparaffinization and dehydration, sections were subjected to hybridization staining according to previously described method31.

Localization analysis
14 days old nodules were embedded in 3% agarose and cut into 70 µm sections using a vibratome (VT1000S, Leica). FM4-64 (5 μg ml−1, from Sigma, F34653) was used to stain the membrane. The cell wall structure was stained with Calcofluor White M2R (0.1%, from Sigma, 910090). Images were acquired with a Leica SP8 confocal microscope with a 63×/1.2 (HC PL APO CS2) water immersion objective and an argon Light Laser (DAPI: 405 nm (ex)/415–465 nm; GFP: 488 nm (ex)/500–550 nm (em); mCherry: 561 nm (ex)/575–630 nm). All the image analyses and projections were performed using either the Fiji32 or Imaris software.

RNA extraction and quantitative real-time PCR
Total RNA was extracted using the Trizol reagent kit (Aidlab Biotechnologies Co., Ltd). The cDNA was synthesized using Hifair II 1st Strand cDNA Synthesis SuperMix (Yeasen Biotech, Shanghai, China). Quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR) was accomplished using Hieff® qPCR SYBR Green Master Mix (No Rox) and CFX Connect real-time PCR detection system (Bio-Rad). The relative expression level was calculated by 2−ΔΔCt (ΔΔCt is the difference of ΔCt between the experimental group and the control group). PP2A was used as the reference gene33. All primers used are listed in Supplementary Table 1.

PGA treatment
For the PGA (Sigma, P3889) treatment S. meliloti 2011 were grown in TY liquid medium at 28°C to OD600 = 1.0, and then 1:100 added to the TY liquid medium containing different doses of PGA (0.1‰, 0.5‰, 1‰ and 2‰). The rhizobia were then incubated at 28°C and the OD600 was measured every 3 h with a spectrophotometer (Eppendorf BioPhotometer D30). For testing S. meliloti 2011 growth on PGA-containing solid plates the S. meliloti 2011 was cultured in TY liquid medium until it reached an OD600 = 1.0, then 10 μL of a dilution series was plated onto TY solid medium containing different concentrations of PGA and incubated at 28°C for 3–4 days. 2‰ PGA was used to treat the rhizobia for scanning electron microscopy analysis.

Scanning electron microscope analysis
Rhizobia were grown overnight in TY liquid medium, then diluted into fresh TY liquid medium with or without PGA (2‰, OD600 = 0.2) culture for 3 h. The rhizobia were then pelleted by centrifugation (1000 × g, 10 min) and washed with 0.01 M PBS buffer (pH 7.0). Immediately after washing, the rhizobia were placed in Formalin-Aceto-Alcohol (from Servicebio, G1103) fixative at 4°C overnight. The overnight fixed samples were dehydrated sequentially for 15–20 min in ethanol solutions of different concentrations (30%, 50%, 70%, 85%, 95%, and 100%), then the dehydrated samples were freeze-dried using a Labogene Scanvac CoolSafe 110-4. Finally, the samples were examined using a scanning electron microscope (FE-SEM, SU8010, HITACHI, Japan).

Live/dead staining
The rhizobial live/dead staining was carried out with solution containing SYTO9 (1:100; from Thermo Fisher, S34854) and PI (1:100, from Solarbio, C0080) in PBS (0.01 M, pH 7.0) for 1–5 min at room temperature. Regarding the nodule sections, the nodules (3 weeks post-inoculation) from the transformed roots of EV, SyPG1/2-RNAi, and SyPG1/2-Cas9 were embedded in 3% agarose. After that, vibratome sections with a thickness of 70 μm were obtained. Immediately, these sections were stained using live/dead staining for 5 min before undergoing microscopy imaging. For PGA and GalA2 treatments: The vibratome sections obtained from wild-type samples were immediately treated with PGA (2‰, from Sigma, P3889) and GalA2 (2, from Macklin, D981325) at room temperature for 3 h before performing live/dead staining for image acquisition. The results were observed using a Leica SP8 confocal microscope as described above.

Statistical analysis
The data were analysed using GraphPad Prism 10 built-in statistical tools.

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

The manuscript titled “Symbiosome functionality in Medicago truncatula nodules requires continuous clearing of pectins from the symbiosome space” by Chen et al. reports that SyPG1 and SyPG2 are localized around symbiosomes. The RNAi knockdown of SyPG1/2 results in early nodule senescence and an excessive accumulation of un-esterified pectin, which in turn inhibits rhizobia growth. While this study is intriguing, more robust results are needed to substantiate their conclusions and warrant publication.
1. The genetic evidence presented is very weak, with only RNAi knockdown and a mild early senescence observed in the SyPG1/2 RNAi nodules, which does not fully support their findings.
2. The accumulation of un-esterified pectin around the symbiosomes in the SyPG1/2 RNAi nodules led the authors to conduct an in vitro assay demonstrating that un-esterified pectin inhibits rhizobia growth. However, there is a significant difference between free-living rhizobia and those within symbiosomes. It is essential to have results from the SyPG1/2 mutants’ nodules to analyze rhizobia growth and activity.
3. Both SyPG1 and SyPG2 are expressed at the apex of mature nodules, yet only the SyPG1/2 RNAi lines exhibit an early senescence phenotype, which should be observed in the nitrogen fixation zone. Additionally, SyPG1 is also localized to the infection threads (IT) and intercellular spaces (ID). This raises the question of whether SyPG1/2 is also necessary for IT formation and/or the release of rhizobia from ITs. To address this, a full analysis of the symbiotic phenotype in SyPG1/2 mutants is required.
4. Given that MsPG3 has been reported in the interaction between M. sativa and rhizobia, but was not mentioned in this manuscript. Is MsPG3 an orthologue of SyPG1/2?

### Reviewer 2

The manuscript by Chen and colleagues, reports a key role for two polygalacturonase genes of Medicago truncatula in the maintenance of rhizobia as nitrogen-fixing organelles in root nodules. Silencing of SyPG1/2 caused the accumulation of un- esterified pectin in the symbiosome space and led to infected nodule cell senescence. Furthermore, they show that un- esterified pectin inhibits rhizobia growth in vitro, affecting rhizobial cell integrity.
The absence of pectins at the cell-wall free symbiosomes has been previously reported. Furthermore, it has been suggested that the plant delivers cell wall degrading enzymes, including enzymes for pectin turnover, to the symbiosomes to prevent the build up of cell wall material in these transient organelles (Gavrin et al., 2016). This work now add more mechanistic insight into this process by identifying two PG genes induced in nodules that contribute to the removal of un-esterified pectin. Furthermore, the data strongly indicate that symbiosome maintenance requires a continuous degradation of homogalacturones in the symbiosome space.
Overall, the manuscript is clearly written and the data largely support the conclusions drawn. Below I have several suggestions:
Surprisingly, the work by Gavrin et al. (2016) is not mentioned in the manuscript. It would be good to include this work in the introduction of the discussion section.
The role of pectin lyases and HGs in the processing of pectin can be clarified better. For example, HGs (first mentioned at line 81) are not properly introduced.
At line 85, a newly identified nodule PME is mentioned. It is not clear how this one was identified? Are these two genes the only PMEs in Medicago? It would be nice to add a phylogenetic analyses (both for PMEs and HGs).
It is not completely clear why the authors focussed on SyPG1 and SyPG2. From the presented public transcriptome data there are additional PGs that seem to be induced in nodules. Do different PGs have different biochemical activities? As additional PGs are highly expressed in the infection zone of the nodule, it raises the question whether these are also involved in the removal of HGs at the symbiosomes. Although it is mentioned that the SyPG1/2 RNAi construct also targets Medtr8g098840 in roots, it should also be tested whether in nodules other PGs might be affected by this construct.
The promoter GUS pattern for SyPG2 does not fit well with the expression profiles of these genes based on publically available RNAseq and gene chip data concerning its expression in the distal infection zone. This is not discussed. It would be good to confirm the expression domains using in situ hybridizations.
At line 185 it is concluded that “Medicago specifically evolved a subset of pectin degrading enzymes that allow spatially confined pectin processing without affecting the extracellular pectin accumulations”. I don’t see any evidence to support the claim that Medicago evolved a specific subset of genes for this purpose. A more evolutionary comparison would be needed to make this claim.
Fig. 1; which promoters are used to express the PME-GFP fusions?
Fig. 3; It would be good to add more detailed (confocal or plastic section) images of the infection zone to compare control vs SyPG1/2 RNAi nodules.
Fig. 4; in panel f LM19 on the y-axis is mentioned, but I guess it has to be LM20 according to the legend.

## Round 1 — Authors' Response

Responses to the reviewers’ comments
We sincerely thank the reviewers for their thoughtful and constructive comments,
which have substantially improved the quality of our manuscript. We have carefully
considered each point raised and implemented the corresponding revisions. A detailed,
point-by-point response is provided below.
In summary, the principal revisions are as follows:
1. The genetic evidence has been strengthened by validating all phenotypic
characteristics (including nodule sections, pectin deposition, and bacterial activity)
through gene editing in hairy roots;
2. The quality of the images has been enhanced by increasing resolution and
generating 3D reconstructions. In addition, Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM)
was employed to examine symbiosomes and pectin deposition;
3. Rhizobial activity has been directly assessed in SyPG1/2-RNAi and SyPG1/2-Cas9
nodules. Furthermore, the effect of PGA (un-esterified pectin) on bacterial activity in
vivo was evaluated by applying the treatment directly to nodule sections;
4. The discussion section has been substantially extended and refined.
REVIEWER COMMENTS
Reviewer #1:
The manuscript titled “Symbiosome functionality in Medicago truncatula nodules
requires continuous clearing of pectins from the symbiosome space” by Chen et al.
reports that SyPG1 and SyPG2 are localized around symbiosomes. The RNAi
knockdown of SyPG1/2 results in early nodule senescence and an excessive
accumulation of un-esterified pectin, which in turn inhibits rhizobia growth. While
this study is intriguing, more robust results are needed to substantiate their
conclusions and warrant publication.
Our response: Thank you very much for the constructive and insightful comments,
which have greatly improved the quality and clarity of our manuscript. We have
carefully considered each point raised, performed additional experiments, and revised
the manuscript accordingly.
Comment 1. The genetic evidence presented is very weak, with only RNAi
knockdown and a mild early senescence observed in the SyPG1/2-RNAi nodules,
which does not fully support their findings.
Our response: We appreciate this important comment. To strengthen our genetic
evidence, we generated CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockout lines specifically targeting
SyPG1 and SyPG2 (SyPG1/2-Cas9). The phenotypes observed in these edited nodules
were consistent with those from the SyPG1/2-RNAi lines, including early senescence
and abnormal pectin deposition (Supplementary Fig. 11 and Supplementary Fig. 13).
These results validate the functional roles of SyPG1 and SyPG2 and provide stronger
genetic support for our conclusions. The new data have been incorporated into the
revised manuscript. We hope that all the new genetic evidences will address your
concerns.
Comment 2. The accumulation of un-esterified pectin around the symbiosomes in the
SyPG1/2-RNAi nodules led the authors to conduct an in vitro assay demonstrating that
un-esterified pectin inhibits rhizobia growth. However, there is a significant difference
between free-living rhizobia and those within symbiosomes. It is essential to have
results from the SyPG1/2 mutants’ nodules to analyze rhizobia growth and activity.
Our response: Thank you for this valuable suggestion. In response, we performed
live/dead staining on nodule sections from both SyPG1/2-RNAi and SyPG1/2-Cas9
transformed roots. These analyses revealed a significant reduction in bacteroid
viability compared with control nodules (Fig. 5i–o and Supplementary Fig. 16).
Furthermore, to directly test the effect of un-esterified pectin on bacteroid activity in
vivo, we applied polygalacturonic acid (PGA) to wild-type (M. truncatula A17)
nodule sections. This treatment also led to a pronounced decrease in bacteroid activity
(Fig. 5h–k). Together, these results confirm that un-esterified pectin compromises
rhizobial activity within nodules, supporting the physiological relevance of our earlier
in vitro findings. We have included these results in the revised manuscript.
Comment 3. Both SyPG1 and SyPG2 are expressed at the apex of mature nodules, yet
only the SyPG1/2-RNAi lines exhibit an early senescence phenotype, which should be
observed in the nitrogen fixation zone. Additionally, SyPG1 is also localized to the
infection threads (IT) and intercellular spaces (ID). This raises the question of whether
SyPG1/2 is also necessary for IT formation and/or the release of rhizobia from ITs. To
address this, a full analysis of the symbiotic phenotype in SyPG1/2 mutants is
required.
Our response: We appreciate this insightful comment. Our results show that although
the promoters of SyPG1 and SyPG2 are active in the apical region of mature nodules,
the encoded proteins exert their principal function within the symbiosome space
located in the interzone, consistent with our in situ hybridization analyses
(Supplementary Fig. 5e–l). We propose that the interzone is the site where pectin
secretion into the symbiosome space occurs; thus, loss of SyPG1/2 function leads to
pectin accumulation in this region, subsequently inducing premature senescence.
To address the infection phenotype, we examined IT morphology in SyPG1/2-RNAi
nodules. No significant differences in IT development were observed compared with
empty vector controls (Supplementary Fig. 10a–b). Although SyPG1 localizes to ITs
and infection droplets (IDs), we did not detect obvious IT defects in the infection zone
of SyPG1/2-RNAi nodules (Supplementary Fig. 10c–d). Enlarged IDs were
occasionally observed, but rhizobial release proceeded normally. These results
indicate that SyPG1/2 is not essential for IT growth or rhizobial release, but it cannot
be ruled out that SyPG1 may have redundant functions with other polygalacturonases
localized to IT and ID. These observations and interpretations are now included in the
revised manuscript.
Comment 4. Given that MsPG3 has been reported in the interaction between M.
sativa and rhizobia, but was not mentioned in this manuscript. Is MsPG3 an
orthologue of SyPG1/2?
Our response: We thank the reviewer for raising this question. Prior to selecting
SyPG1/2 as candidate genes, we conducted a phylogenetic analysis including MsPG3.
Our results indicate that MsPG3 and SyPG1/2 do not belong to the same evolutionary
clade (Supplementary Fig. 3). Furthermore, transcriptomic data show that PGs
clustering with MsPG3 are not expressed during rhizobial inoculation in M.
truncatula (see below). Taken together, these results demonstrate that SyPG1/2 are
not orthologues of MsPG3.

homogalacturonan (HG) removal at this site. While we cannot exclude the possibility

SyPG1/2-Cas9 lines recapitulated the RNAi phenotypes (Supplementary Fig. 11),
